title: The Last Lesson
summary: Set in a French village of Alsace after the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71, the story describes the day an order from Berlin ends the teaching of French in local schools. Through young Franz and his teacher M. Hamel, Alphonse Daudet shows how deeply people value their language only when they are about to lose it.

notes.heading: About the author
notes.html: Alphonse Daudet (1840–1897) was a French novelist and short-story writer known for gentle humour and sympathetic portraits of ordinary people. The story comes from his collection of tales about the Franco-Prussian War.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: Franz, a careless schoolboy, arrives late expecting a scolding, but finds the classroom solemn and village elders sitting on the back benches. M. Hamel announces that this is the last French lesson, since Prussian rulers have ordered that only German be taught in Alsace and Lorraine. Franz suddenly regrets his neglect of French, listens with full attention, and the lesson ends with M. Hamel, too moved to speak, writing a patriotic salute to France on the blackboard.

notes.heading: Detailed summary
notes.html:
The late morning. Franz is late for school and dreads being questioned on participles, which he has not learnt. He is tempted to spend the day outdoors watching Prussian soldiers drill, but resists. Passing the town hall, he sees a crowd at the bulletin board, the place where all bad news of the last two years has been posted.

An unusual classroom. Normally school opens with a din of desks and lessons chanted aloud, under which Franz hoped to slip in. Today it is as quiet as a Sunday. M. Hamel, instead of scolding, kindly asks him to take his seat. He is wearing his best green coat, frilled shirt and embroidered black silk cap, kept for inspections and prize days. On the back benches sit old Hauser, the former mayor, the former postmaster and others, looking sad.

The announcement. M. Hamel explains that an order has come from Berlin: from tomorrow only German will be taught in Alsace and Lorraine, and a new master will arrive. This is their last French lesson. Franz is shocked. His books, which once felt a nuisance, now seem like old friends, and he feels sorry for having wasted time on bird-nesting and sliding on the Saar.

The lesson. When Franz cannot recite the participle rule, M. Hamel does not scold him. Instead he reflects that everyone in Alsace has postponed learning, parents sending children to work in mills and he himself giving holidays or sending pupils to water his flowers. He praises French as the most beautiful, clear and logical language in the world and urges them to guard it, because a people who keep their language hold the key to their prison.

The last moments. Franz understands everything with surprising ease. There is a writing lesson with new copies bearing ‘France’ and ‘Alsace’, which hang like little flags. Even the pigeons coo softly, and Franz wonders whether the Prussians will make them sing in German too. Old Hauser joins in the spelling with his spectacles and primer, voice trembling. When the church clock strikes twelve and the Prussian trumpets sound, M. Hamel rises, pale, cannot speak, writes a salute to France in large letters on the board, and signals that school is dismissed.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• Linguistic chauvinism and loss of identity: the conquerors impose German to erase French identity; language is tied to freedom and pride.
  • Procrastination: people realise the value of things only when they are lost; Franz, the parents and M. Hamel all postponed learning.
  • Patriotism: love for one’s country expressed through love for one’s mother tongue.
  • Pathos of war: war affects not just soldiers but children, teachers and old villagers.

notes.heading: Character sketches
notes.html:
Franz: a lively, careless boy who prefers the outdoors to grammar. In the course of one morning he matures, feeling regret, respect for his teacher and love for French. His innocent wonder about the pigeons carries the story’s irony.

M. Hamel: a strict but devoted teacher who has taught for forty years. On the last day he is gentle, dignified and patriotic, honest enough to admit his own faults, and heartbroken at having to leave. His silent farewell shows feeling too deep for words.

The village elders: represent the community’s guilt and grief; they come to thank the master and pay respect to a country that is no longer theirs.

notes.heading: Title justification
notes.html: The title is apt because the whole story centres on the final French lesson taught in the village school. ‘Last’ carries emotional weight: it is the last lesson for M. Hamel as a teacher, for the students in their mother tongue, and symbolically the last day of French cultural freedom in Alsace.

notes.heading: Message and values
notes.html: We should value our language, culture and opportunities while we have them and not put off learning till tomorrow. The story also warns against the arrogance of conquerors who try to rule people by taking away their language.

keyTerms.definition: A verb form used as an adjective (e.g. broken, singing); the grammar topic Franz had not learnt.
Notice board at the town hall where war news and orders of the Prussian command were posted.
French districts annexed by Prussia after the war of 1870–71; the setting of the story.
Aggressive belief in the superiority of one’s own language and its imposition on others.
A small elementary book for learning to read; old Hauser brought his to class.
The habit of postponing work; the story’s chief human failing.
Contrast between expectation and reality, e.g. Franz expects punishment but receives kindness; he loves French only when it is taken away.
A quality that evokes pity and sorrow, felt in M. Hamel’s silent farewell.

mcqs.q: Why was Franz afraid of going to school that morning?
options: He had not done his writing homework.
M. Hamel would question him on participles, which he had not learnt.
mcqs.explanation: Franz dreaded being questioned on participles, a topic he did not know at all.

mcqs.q: What was unusual about the classroom when Franz entered?
options: It was as quiet as a Sunday morning.
mcqs.explanation: Normally there was a great bustle, but that day everything was still, like a Sunday morning, a sign of something serious.

mcqs.q: Why were the village elders sitting on the back benches?
options: They wanted to inspect the school.
They had come to learn German.
They came to thank M. Hamel and show respect to the country that was no longer theirs.
mcqs.explanation: The elders came to honour M. Hamel’s forty years of service and express grief at losing their language and country.

mcqs.q: The order from Berlin stated that:
options: only German would be taught in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine
French would be taught twice a day
mcqs.explanation: The order made German the only language to be taught in Alsace and Lorraine, replacing French.

mcqs.q: M. Hamel’s special dress that day was worn usually on:
mcqs.explanation: His green coat, frilled shirt and silk cap were reserved for inspection and prize days; wearing them showed the day’s significance.

mcqs.q: According to M. Hamel, who was responsible for the neglect of French?
options: The students, the parents and he himself
mcqs.explanation: M. Hamel admits that everyone shared the blame: students postponed study, parents sent children to work, and he gave holidays.

mcqs.q: What did M. Hamel say about a people who keep their language?
options: They hold the key to their freedom even when enslaved.
mcqs.explanation: He compared language to the key to a prison: as long as people hold on to it, they keep their identity and hope of freedom.

mcqs.q: Franz’s question about whether the pigeons would be made to sing in German shows:
options: the absurdity of imposing a language on people
mcqs.explanation: The innocent question exposes the absurdity and cruelty of linguistic imposition; one cannot force nature, or people’s hearts, to change language.

mcqs.q: Why could M. Hamel not finish his final sentence at the end?
mcqs.explanation: He was choked with emotion, so he wrote his salute to France on the blackboard instead.

mcqs.q: What does the bulletin board symbolise in the story?
options: Bad news and orders of the occupying power
mcqs.explanation: For two years the bulletin board had carried news of lost battles, drafts and orders, so it stood for bad news from the Prussian rulers.

questions.q:
Read the situation and answer: Franz describes how, on that last day, his books on grammar and history no longer seemed a nuisance but felt like old friends he could not bear to give up.
(a) What had Franz felt about these books earlier? (1)
(b) What brought about this change? (1)
(c) Which literary device is used when books are called ‘old friends’? (1)
(d) What does this moment reveal about Franz? (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) He had found them a nuisance and heavy to carry.

(b) The news that this was the last French lesson made him realise he would never be taught in French again.

(c) Metaphor (the books are personified as friends).

(d) It reveals his sudden maturity and regret for having wasted time.

questions.q: What changes did the order from Berlin cause in the school that day?
questions.answerHtml: The order turned the noisy classroom solemn and silent. M. Hamel dressed in his finest clothes and spoke kindly instead of scolding. Village elders sat on the back benches, and students and teacher alike gave the lesson full attention, aware it was the last.

questions.q: How did Franz’s feelings about M. Hamel change?
questions.answerHtml: Franz had feared M. Hamel and his iron ruler. On learning that the master was leaving forever, he forgot the scoldings and felt sorrow and sympathy for him. He now saw him as a devoted teacher whose departure was a real loss.

questions.q: Why does M. Hamel say that parents and he himself were to blame for the students’ poor French?
questions.answerHtml: Parents preferred their children to earn a little money in farms and mills rather than study. M. Hamel admitted he had sent pupils to water his flowers and given them holidays when he wanted to go fishing, so learning had always been put off.

questions.q: ‘The Last Lesson’ shows that people often realise the value of what they have only when it is about to be lost. Discuss with reference to Franz, the villagers and M. Hamel. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Daudet’s story turns on the painful truth that we value things only when we are losing them. Franz had treated French lessons as a burden, preferring to chase birds and slide on the Saar. The moment he learns that French will no longer be taught, his dull grammar books become dear friends and he wishes he had learnt his participles.

The villagers, who once sent their children to work in mills instead of school, now crowd the back benches, sad and guilty, to attend a lesson they had never cared for. Old Hauser’s trembling recitation shows their grief.

Even M. Hamel admits he gave holidays too easily. On his last day he teaches with unusual patience and is too moved to speak at the end. Thus the impending loss transforms indifference into love for the mother tongue and the nation, a lesson that procrastination can cost us dearly.

questions.q: Write a character sketch of M. Hamel. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
M. Hamel is the village schoolmaster who has taught in Alsace for forty years. Normally strict, he keeps a ruler under his arm and is feared by careless pupils like Franz. Yet on the last day he reveals a gentle and dignified side, welcoming the late Franz kindly and teaching with remarkable patience.

He is deeply patriotic. He dresses in his ceremonial clothes to honour the occasion and speaks of French as the most beautiful and logical language, urging his pupils to guard it because it is the key to their freedom. He is honest too, admitting that he himself had sometimes neglected his duty.

His love for his school and country is touching. Leaving after forty years breaks his heart, and when the trumpets of the Prussians sound, he cannot speak; he simply writes a salute to France on the board. He remains a symbol of devotion and quiet courage.
